text: Saving state so a run can resume is only half the story. This lesson covers how a job detects a failure, reacts to it, and gets back to training with minimal lost time -- without a human having to notice and restart it by hand.

A thousand GPUs running for two weeks has a much higher chance that some GPU in the fleet fails before the run completes, just from the sheer number of components involved. Major training runs routinely see multiple hardware failures a day. So the training loop has to assume interruption is coming: a stuck collective communication gets caught by a timeout and turned into a visible error, an elastic agent restarts the failed workers automatically, and a rendezvous step reconnects the survivors so training resumes from the last checkpoint.

A crash is the easy case -- the process dies and the scheduler notices right away. The harder case is a silent hang, where a GPU or network link degrades without crashing, and an all-reduce during gradient sync blocks forever waiting on a rank that will never respond. Without an explicit timeout on the process group, the whole job just appears frozen with no error at all.

PyTorch's elastic launcher through torchrun handles this: a node range lets the job continue with fewer nodes if some drop out, max-restarts bounds how many times it will automatically retry failed workers, and the rendezvous backend lets surviving workers find each other again after a restart. On restart, training resumes from the last checkpoint -- which is why checkpoint cadence and fault tolerance are really one system, not two separate concerns.

Beyond timeouts, production stacks run periodic health checks so a degrading node gets flagged and drained before it stalls the whole job. But not every failure looks like a crash or a hang -- next lesson covers the node that doesn't die, it just falls behind everyone else.
